Who is this? Family, age, honorifics
to attend on a regular basis / to work for

There are five people in my family: grandma, dad, mum, my older sister and me. Grandma is eighty this year. She takes a walk in the park every morning. Dad is an office worker and mum is a middle school teacher. My sister is 28. She is really good at cooking. And we have a puppy too!

Steven: Hello! Nice to meet you.
Minsu: Nice to meet you. You speak Korean really well!
Steven: Not at all. I'm still not good at it.
Older brother / older sister depends on YOU
Korean names older siblings differently for men and women:
**의** links an owner to a thing: **친구의 가방** (a friend's bag). In speech 의 is often dropped: **친구 가방**. Pronounced [에].
My older sister's husband is a reporter.
Always contract: **제** 동생 (my younger sibling), not ~~저의 동생~~ in speech. For family Koreans often say **우리**: 우리 어머니.

Age, people and things are counted with native numbers. After 10 (열) come new words for the tens:
Tens + units: 25 = **스물다섯**. Before 살/명 the short forms are used: 한, 두, 세, 네, **스무** (20): **스무 살**, 스물한 살.
About older people use **연세** (age) instead of 나이 and **분** (person) instead of 명: 손님이 세 **분** 계세요.
Koreans used to count age differently (“Korean age”: +1 or +2). Since 2023 official documents use the international age.
How many people are in your family?
How many people are in your family and how old are they?
Good / not good at: N을/를 잘하다
**N을/를 잘해요** = I'm good at N. **잘 못해요** = I'm not very good. **못해요** = I can't (at all).
When praised, Koreans usually deny it: **뭘요. 아직 잘 못해요.** — Not at all, I'm still not good.

Never use -(으)시- about yourself: ~~제가 가세요~~ → 제가 가요.

What time is it? Time, schedules, plans

Nana, how have you been? Are you free this weekend? On Saturday I'm going to Yeouido with a friend. We'll rent bikes there and ride along the Han River from 2 to 5 pm. In the evening we'll eat in Gangnam. Come with us! Please reply. — Michael
Seoul Museum: Tue–Sun 9 am – 6 pm, closed on Mondays. Immigration Office: Mon–Fri 9 am – 6 pm, lunch break 12–1.

Yujin gets up at 6:30. After getting up she takes a shower. Around 7 she has breakfast and at 8 takes the bus. She has classes from 9 to 12. In the afternoon she studies in the library. She goes to bed at 11 pm.
Hours are native, minutes are Sino-Korean
Hours use **native** numbers (한, 두, 세…), minutes use **Sino-Korean** ones (십, 이십…). Half past = **반**, about = **쯤**.
**오전** a.m., **오후** p.m.; more exactly: 새벽 (early morning) → 아침 (morning) → 낮 (daytime) → 저녁 (evening) → 밤 (night). Time + **에**: 아침 여덟 시**에** 일어나요.
4 o'clock is 네 시, not 넷 시; 20 minutes is 이십 분, not 스무 분.
Let's meet around six in the evening.
I go to bed at 11 pm.
What time do you usually get up?
**부터** marks the start, **까지** the end. Works with hours, days and dates.
I have classes Monday to Friday.
Only one end is fine too
세 시까지 와요. (Come by three.) / 내일부터 운동해요. (I'll exercise from tomorrow.)
For places (from Seoul to Busan) another pair is used: 에서 … 까지 — see unit 13.
From 7 pm I use the computer.
After getting up in the morning I wash my face.
I work from nine to six.
I call my mother on Sundays.
What does Yujin do right after getting up?
Describe your weekday schedule using 부터 … 까지.
When the second action depends on the first
**-아서/어서** links two actions that share a place, person or object: you meet a friend **and (with that friend)** watch a movie; you buy an apple **and eat (that apple)**.
I met a friend and (together) we watched a movie.
I went to Gangnam and shopped there.
I made a cake and gave it to a friend.
**-고** just lists actions in order: 밥을 먹고 커피를 마셨어요. **-아서/어서** is needed when the first action is the basis for the second: ~~학교에 가고 공부해요~~ → **학교에 가서 공부해요** (study at the school you went to).
I get up and wash my face.
Like -고, -아서/어서 never takes the past tense itself: ~~갔어서~~ → 가서 …했어요.
“I went to the museum and saw paintings (there).”
You eat the same apple you bought — the actions are connected.
I went to Gangnam and met a friend there.
I went to Yeouido and rode a bike.
I got up and took a shower.
I waited for the bus and then took it.
What will Michael do in Yeouido?
rent bikes and ride along the river
bought a book at the bookstore
went to the bookstore, then home
What did you do last weekend? Use -아서/어서 once.
Vowel stem + **-ㄹ 거예요**, consonant stem + **-을 거예요**, ㄹ-stem + **거예요**.
What will you do this weekend?
During the vacation I'll learn to drive.
After the future -ㄹ, the next ㄱ ㄷ ㅂ ㅅ ㅈ become tense: **갈 거예요 [갈 꺼예요]**, **먹을 거예요 [머글 꺼예요]**.
Formal: -(으)ㄹ 겁니다 / 것입니다: 내일 출발할 겁니다.
What are you going to do this weekend?
I'm going to Jeonju this weekend.
Where will they eat in the evening?
What will you do this weekend? Name two plans.
Practice: plans by e-mail · opening hours
Greeting (**잘 지냈어요?**) → the plan with **-(으)ㄹ 거예요** and **부터/까지** → invitation (**같이 가요!**) → **답장 주세요** (please reply).
Signs often use ~ for “from … to”: 오전 9시 ~ 오후 6시 = 오전 아홉 시부터 오후 여섯 시까지. **쉽니다** = closed.
그렇지만 = but (at the start of a sentence), the same as 하지만.
Until when is the Immigration Office open?
Can you go to the Immigration Office on Saturday?
What does Michael ask Nana to do?
How have you been? Please reply.
This vacation I'm going to Jeonju.
Reply to Michael's e-mail: can you go? what will you do? (use -(으)ㄹ 거예요 and 부터/까지)
Tell your plans for the next vacation.
**Hours** take native numbers (한 시, 두 시 … 열두 시); **minutes** take Sino-Korean numbers (십 분, 삼십 분). Half past = **반**. About = **쯤**: 세 시쯤.

1. ~~이 시 열 분~~ → **두** 시 **십** 분. 2. -아서/어서 never takes the past: ~~만났어서~~ → 만나**서** 영화를 **봤어요**. 3. Use -아서/어서 when the second action needs the first (가서, 만나서, 사서, 만들어서); use -고 for a plain sequence (먹고 자요). 4. ~~먹ㄹ 거예요~~ → 먹**을** 거예요; ~~살을 거예요~~ → **살** 거예요.

I will rest at home tomorrow.

I work from nine to six. At the weekend I'll meet a friend and have fun.

I caught a cold: body, symptoms, advice
to be prevalent / to be spread
aches and pains due to the flu

Colds are going around these days. Since yesterday I've had a fever and a cough. My throat hurts and I have a runny nose. My friend told me: “You must drink a lot of warm water and get plenty of rest. Don't drink ice water. Don't overdo it today.” So today I'm not going to class; I'm resting at home.

When Koreans catch a cold, they do this: for a sore throat — rinse the mouth with warm salt water; for a cough — drink radish juice; for a stuffy nose — put green onion next to the nose; for body aches — massage the shoulders.
**N이/가 아파요** = my N hurts. Question: **어디가 아파요?**
**배** = belly (also pear, ship!), **목** = neck and throat, **다리** = leg (and bridge).
A children's song helps: 머리 어깨 무릎 발 무릎 발 — head, shoulders, knees and toes.
I've had a headache since yesterday.
Imagine you're at a doctor's. Say what hurts.
If a stem ends in **ㅡ**, the ㅡ disappears before -아요/어요. Which ending? Look at the syllable **before** it: ㅏ/ㅗ → **-아요**, otherwise **-어요**. One-syllable stems take **-어요**.
**감기에 걸렸어요** — I caught a cold. **열이 나요** — I have a fever. **기침을 해요** — I cough. **콧물이 나요** — I have a runny nose. **몸살이 났어요** — I ache all over.
Most of these verbs describe states; with past -았/었- they mean “have become”: 감기에 걸렸어요 = I have a cold (now).
I'm coughing and have a runny nose.
I caught a cold and have a fever.
You have a cold. Describe your symptoms (2 symptoms).
Stem + **-지 마세요** = please don't … (polite). Formal signs: **-지 마십시오**.
**안 가요** describes (I'm not going). **가지 마세요** asks someone not to go.
Sign language: 사진을 찍지 마십시오 (no photos), 들어가지 마십시오 (no entry).
Don't go to the PC room.
Don't drink ice water. Drink warm water.
What did the friend say NOT to do?
Give two “don't” rules for someone with a cold.
“Have to / must”: take the -아요/어요 form, replace 요 with **야 되다**: 먹어요 → **먹어야 돼요**, 가요 → **가야 돼요**, 해요 → **해야 돼요**. (**하다** is also possible: 먹어야 해요.)
I have to hand in the report by tomorrow.
You need to get plenty of rest.
**만** replaces 이/가 and 을/를: 물**만** 마셨어요 (I drank only water). Other particles stay: 집**에서만** 쉬어요.
The opposite, “don't have to”: -지 않아도 돼요 (2A).
It's grandma's birthday next week (polite word).
You need to drink lots of warm water.
I need to practise Korean pronunciation.
You have to rest well and wash your hands.
has to get married next year
A friend has a cold. Give two pieces of advice with -아야/어야 돼요.
When ㅎ meets ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅈ (on either side), they merge into ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, ㅊ:
Korean home remedies use everyday things: **소금물** (salt water), **무즙** (radish juice), **파** (green onion), **마사지** (massage).
What do Koreans do for a sore throat?
put green onion on the nose
Got it. I have to drink warm water.
It's okay. I've got much better.
A friend has a cold. Write advice: what they must do and what they shouldn't do.
What do people in your country do when they catch a cold?
Before -아/어 the vowel ㅡ drops; then look at the vowel before it: ㅏ or ㅗ → **-아**, otherwise **-어**. One-syllable stems take **-어**.

1. ~~아프어요~~ → 아**파**요; ~~예쁘아요~~ → 예**뻐**요. 2. Before a consonant nothing drops: 아프**지만**, 바쁘**고**, 아**픕**니다. 3. ~~안 가세요~~ for “don't go” → 가**지 마세요**. 4. 만 replaces 을/를 and 이/가: 물**만** 마셔요; with other particles it follows: 집에서**만**. 5. 되다 → **돼요**: 가야 **돼요**.
“I have a fever and a cough.”
My throat hurts. So please don't talk much.
I've caught a cold. I must rest well at home.
In the morning I drink only coffee.
Don't overdo it. You must go to bed early.
a cold: fever and sore throat; medicine, rest, no alcohol
too busy today — a report to write and hand in
I've caught a cold and my throat hurts. Today I must rest at home.
A friend has a cold. Say what hurts (as the friend), then give two “musts” and two “don'ts”.

Excuse me, but who's calling, please?

Clerk: Hello, Seoul Travel Agency.
Nana: Hello. This is Kim Minsu's office, isn't it?
Clerk: Yes, it is. Excuse me, who's calling?
Nana: I'm Park Nana. May I speak to Minsu?
Clerk: Minsu is in a meeting now. Please call again later.
Yujin, sorry. I overslept this morning so I couldn't go to class. What was the homework? Also, I don't know where next week's exam is, so I'm texting you. Please reply! — Akira
In Korea, if there is a fire or an accident, call 119. If there is a burglary, call 112. Foreigners can call 1345 and get help in many languages.
**여보세요?** — hello (only on the phone). **거기 N이지요?** — Is this N? **실례지만 누구세요?** — Excuse me, who is calling? **N 좀 바꿔 주세요** — May I speak to N?
Hello? Is this Seoul Travel Agency?
Digit by digit with Sino-Korean numbers; 0 = **공**, the dash is read **에**: 010-2345-6789 → 공일공에 이삼사오에 육칠팔구.
전화를 하다 = to make a call, 전화를 받다 = to answer a call.
What do you say when you pick up the phone?
0 in a phone number is read …
A friend called me earlier (I answered).
Hello? Is this Seoul Travel Agency?
Say your phone number aloud (or make one up).
Stem + **-지요?** asks the listener to confirm something you believe: 날씨가 덥**지요**? — It's hot, isn't it? In speech often **-죠?**. Past: **-았지요/었지요?**
Korean food is tasty, isn't it?
You took the exam yesterday, right?
After a consonant **이지요?**, after a vowel **지요?**: 학생**이지요**? 의사**지요**? On the phone: 거기 여행사**지요**?
그럼요 = of course! 다른 = other, different: 다른 장소 (another place).
With a noun ending in a consonant:
The food here is bad, isn't it?
Shall we meet at another place?
How does Nana check that she called the right place?
The food there is bad, right?
Ask a friend to confirm two things with -지요?
Stem + **-고 있어요** = is doing right now. Past **-고 있었어요** = was doing. Honorific: **-고 계세요**.
What are you doing right now?
Did you call earlier? I was taking a shower then.
The boss is in a meeting.
Simple -아요/어요 is often enough. Use -고 있다 to stress “right at this moment” or “in the middle of”.
아까 / 조금 전 = a little while ago; 이따(가) = a little later.
I got a text a little while ago.
A friend calls: 지금 뭐 하고 있어요? Answer.
**못** = can't (for some reason), while **안** = don't (by choice). Noun + 하다 verbs: 운동**을 못 해요** / 운동 **못 해요**.
I'm not going (I don't want to)
I'm busy so I can't go.

The same ending as in unit 10, but here it means **because**: 늦잠을 **자서** 늦었어요. The first part never takes the past tense: ~~늦잠을 잤어서~~.

“I was sick, so I couldn't come.”
My stomach hurt so I couldn't eat.
I couldn't finish all my homework.

To Seoul Station, please: transport, favours, plans

Not long ago I went to Gyeongju alone. I was going to take the train at Seoul Station, but I got lost inside the station. A lady helped me then. She bought me a ticket and even walked me to the train. I was really grateful. The next day I texted her from Gyeongju.

In Seoul a transport card is very convenient. You can take buses and the subway with it. If you transfer from the subway to a bus, the fare is cheaper. You have to tap the card when you get off too. You can buy a card at a convenience store.
**로** after a vowel or ㄹ, **으로** after other consonants. With transport it means “by”: **버스로**, **지하철로**, **배로**.
How do you get to school?
I went to Busan by train.
With 가다/오다 it also means “towards”: **서울역으로 가 주세요** (to Seoul Station, please). Compare 에 (to a point) — both are fine with 가다.
**N을/를 타다** — get on / ride, **N에서 내리다** — get off at N, **N에서 갈아타다** — transfer at N.
Transfer to line 2 at City Hall station.
Where do you wait for a bus?
I go to school by bike.
I changed trains at City Hall station.
How do you get to school?
I went to Busan by express bus.
How does the speaker get to work?
take a taxi in front of the train station

From … to …: N에서 N까지 · how long
For places: **에서** = from, **까지** = to. (For time it was 부터 … 까지.)
Is it far from home to school?
